facts.statement: The genus Compagopiscis was described by Gardiner and Miles in 1994.
Compagopiscis lived during the Upper Devonian (Frasnian stage) in Western Australia.
facts.quote: It lived in the Upper Devonian (Frasnian stage) of Western Australia.

facts.statement: Compagopiscis is a monotypic genus containing only the species Compagopiscis croucheri.
facts.quote: The genus is monotypic, with its only species being Compagopiscis croucheri.

facts.statement: Compagopiscis is recognized as one of the earliest known vertebrates to possess teeth.
facts.quote: Compagopiscis is one of the earliest known vertebrates to have teeth.

facts.statement: Analysis of its bite force suggests Compagopiscis was a generalist predator with a diverse diet.
facts.quote: An analysis of its bite force suggests that it was a generalist predator, having a diverse diet.

facts.statement: The abundance of fossils suggests that Compagopiscis may have exhibited schooling behavior.
facts.quote: Fossils have been found in numbers, suggesting possible schooling behavior.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis places Compagopiscis within the clade Coccosteomorphi, part of the superfamily Incisoscutoidea and the group Eubrachythoraci.
facts.quote: Torosteus is now considered to be a member of the superfamily Incisoscutoidea, which belongs to the clade Coccosteomorphi, one of the two major clades within Eubrachythoraci.

facts.statement: The parent group for Compagopiscis is the family Panxiosteidae.
Compagopiscis is classified within the class Placodermi.
Compagopiscis lived between 382.31 and 372.15 million years ago during the Frasnian stage.
